claim: Healthy volunteers practiced preferentially at a peak time of approximately 15:00.
source: Circular statistics within each group demonstrated that HV practiced preferentially at a peak time of ~15:00 (mean resultant length 0.47, p = 0.000497, Rayleigh test for the uniformity of a circular distribution of points; Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by circular statistics (Rayleigh test) showing non-uniform distribution with specific peak time, with reference to Figure 2b.

claim: OCD participants had a preferred practice time with a mean direction at approximately 18:00.
source: For OCD participants, the preferred practice time had a mean direction at ~18:00 (mean resultant length 0.58, p = 8.03 × 10–6, Rayleigh test; Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by circular statistics (Rayleigh test) showing non-uniform distribution with specific peak time, with reference to Figure 2c.

claim: There were no significant differences in daily training patterns between OCD patients and healthy volunteers.
source: There were, however, no significant differences between both samples (p = 0.19, Watson's U2 test).
evidence: Supported by Watson's U2 test comparing circular distributions between groups showing non-significant result (p = 0.19).

claim: OCD patients do not exhibit learning deficits in motor sequence acquisition.
source: The results indicate that OCD patients do not exhibit learning deficits. While they initially performed action sequences slower than the HV group, their learning rates ultimately matched those of HV. Both groups showed comparable movement durations at the asymptote.
evidence: Based on inference from the statistical analyses showing similar learning rates and asymptotic performance between groups, despite initial differences in baseline performance.

claim: Compared to healthy volunteers, OCD patients took significantly longer to achieve a similar level of automaticity in both reward schedules.
source: In conclusion, compared to HV, patients took significantly longer to achieve a similar level of automaticity in both reward schedules. They began at a slower pace, exhibited more variability, and progressed to automaticity at a slower rate.
evidence: Based on inference from the statistical analyses showing significant group differences in automaticity rate (nC) and amount of automation gain (CL), while achieving similar asymptotic levels.

claim: Both OCD and healthy volunteer participants speeded up their sequence performance more following a drop in scores than following an increase in scores.
source: We observed that participants speeded up their sequence duration more (negative changes in trial-wise MT) following a drop in scores, as expected (Figure 5a). Conducting a three-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with reward change (increase, decrease) and bin (1:4, each bin denoting ~110 sequences) as within-subject factors, and group as between-subject factor, we found a significant main effect of reward (F (504,1) = 319.383, p = 2.0 × 10–16).
evidence: Supported by three-way ANOVA showing significant main effect of reward (p = 2.0 × 10–16), with reference to Figure 5a.

claim: Participants sped up their sequence performance over the course of practice sessions.
source: There was also a significant main effect of bin (F (504,3) = 19.583, p = 5.06 × 10–12), such that participants sped up their sequence performance over practices.
evidence: Supported by three-way ANOVA showing significant main effect of bin (p = 5.06 × 10–12).

claim: OCD and healthy volunteer individuals introduced comparable changes in movement time overall during training.
source: There was no significant main group effect (F (504,1) = 1.099, p = 0.2951) and omitting the group factor from the full model using a BF ANOVA improved the model moderately (BF = 6.08, moderate evidence in support of the model with the main group effect removed relative to the full model). Thus, both OCD and HV individuals introduced comparable changes in MT overall during training.
evidence: Supported by three-way ANOVA showing non-significant group effect (p = 0.2951) and Bayesian analysis providing moderate evidence (BF = 6.08) for absence of group effect.

claim: The relative improvement in movement time over sequences depended on whether the reward increased or decreased from the previous trial.
source: In addition, there was a significant interaction between reward and bin in predicting the trial-to-trial changes in movement time (F (504,3) = 3.652, p = 0.0126). This outcome suggested that the relative improvement in MT over sequences depended on whether the reward increased or decreased from the previous trial.
evidence: Supported by three-way ANOVA showing significant reward × bin interaction (p = 0.0126).

claim: In each sequence bin, participants speeded up movement time more following a drop in scores than following an increment.
source: To explore this interaction effect further, we conducted a dependent-sample pairwise t-test on MT, after collapsing the data across groups. In each sequence bin, participants speeded up MT more following a drop in scores than following an increment, as expected (corrected pFDR = 2 × 10–16).
evidence: Supported by post-hoc pairwise t-tests showing significant differences (corrected pFDR = 2 × 10–16) between reward increase and decrease conditions.

claim: The large sensitivity of normalized movement time changes to reward decrements was attenuated from the first to the second bin of practice.
source: On the other hand, assessing the effect of bins separately for each level of reward, we observed that the large sensitivity of normalized MT changes to reward decrements was attenuated from the first to the second bin of practice (corrected pFDR = 0.00034, significant attenuation for pairs 1–2; dependent-sample t-tests between consecutive pairs of bins). No further changes over practice bins were observed (p > 0.53, no change for pairs 2–3, 3–4).
evidence: Supported by post-hoc pairwise t-tests showing significant change between bins 1-2 (corrected pFDR = 0.00034) but not between subsequent bins.

claim: The standard deviation of the distribution of trial-to-trial movement time changes was smaller in healthy volunteers than in OCD patients.
source: Assessment of the std (σ) of the Gaussian distributions p(∆T|∆R−) and p(∆T|∆R+) in the continuous reward condition (Figure 5c) with a similar three-way ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of group (F (504,1) = 19.928, p = 9.93 × 10–6). As shown in Figure 5d, the std (σ) of the distribution of trial-to-trial MT changes was smaller in HV than in OCD.
evidence: Supported by three-way ANOVA showing significant main effect of group (p = 9.93 × 10–6) on standard deviation, with reference to Figures 5c and 5d.

claim: Over the course of training, both groups exhibited less variable changes in movement time in response to both reward increments and decrements.
source: In addition, we observed a significant change over bins of sequences in σ, and independently of the group or reward factors (main effect of bin, F (504,3) = 39.078, p = 2 × 10–16). This outcome reflected that over the course of training, both groups exhibited less variable changes in MT in response to both reward increments and decrements, in line with improvements in skill learning (Wolpert et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by three-way ANOVA showing significant main effect of bin (p = 2 × 10–16) on standard deviation, with citation to skill learning literature (Wolpert et al., 2011).

claim: Reward decrements were associated with a more variable distribution of behavioral changes than reward increments.
source: Reward also modulated σ, with ∆R− being associated with a more variable distribution of behavioral changes than ∆R+(main effect of reward, F (504,1) = 17.110, p = 4.13 × 10–05).
evidence: Supported by three-way ANOVA showing significant main effect of reward (p = 4.13 × 10–05) on standard deviation.

claim: Both OCD patients and healthy controls exhibited an increased consistency of IKI patterns trial to trial across bins of correct sequences during continuous reward practices.
source: During continuous reward practices, both patients and healthy controls exhibited an increased consistency of IKI patterns trial to trial across bins of correct sequences (decreased normC, Equation 8, Figure 6a; main effect of bin on the center of the Gaussian distribution, F (497, 3) = 4.188, p = 0.00607; three-way ANOVA).
evidence: Supported by three-way ANOVA showing significant main effect of bin (p = 0.00607) on IKI consistency, with reference to Figure 6a.

claim: OCD patients had less consistent timing patterns trial to trial compared to healthy volunteers.
source: Performance in OCD and HV, however, differed with regard to how reproducible their timing patterns were (main effect of group, F (497, 1) = 8.130, p = 0.00454). The timing patterns were less consistent trial to trial in OCD, relative to HV (Figure 6b, left panel).
evidence: Supported by three-way ANOVA showing significant main effect of group (p = 0.00454) on IKI consistency, with reference to Figure 6b.

claim: IKI consistency improved more following reward increments than after decrements.
source: Moreover, the IKI consistency improved more (smaller normC) following reward increments than after decrements, as shown in Figure 6b (right panel; main reward effect, F (497, 1) = 23.283, p = 1.86 × 10–6).
evidence: Supported by three-way ANOVA showing significant main effect of reward (p = 1.86 × 10–6) on IKI consistency, with reference to Figure 6b.

claim: The standard deviation of the Gaussian distribution for normalized IKI consistency values was reduced across bins of practiced sequences.
source: Regarding the spread of the p(∆T|∆R) distributions, we found a significant main effect of bin factor (F (504,3) = 23.350, p = 3.63 × 10–14; Figure 6c and d). These outcomes suggest that the σ of the Gaussian distribution for normC values was reduced across bins of practiced sequences.
evidence: Supported by three-way ANOVA showing significant main effect of bin (p = 3.63 × 10–14) on standard deviation of IKI consistency, with reference to Figures 6c and 6d.

claim: When given the option to play an easier-but-shorter sequence, both OCD patients and healthy volunteers significantly preferred it over the app familiar sequence.
source: However, when given the option to play an easier-but-shorter sequence (in experimental condition 2), both groups significantly preferred it over the app familiar sequence (Figure 7b, right plot).
evidence: Based on inference from the statistical analysis showing significant difference between experimental condition 2 and other conditions, with reference to Figure 7b.

claim: Participants with greater habitual tendencies had a greater propensity to prefer the trained app sequence when choosing between the app sequence and a shorter alternative.
source: A positive correlation between COHS and the app sequence choice (Pearson r = 0.36, p = 0.005) showed that those participants with greater habitual tendencies had a greater propensity to prefer the trained app sequence under this condition.
evidence: Supported by Pearson correlation analysis showing significant positive correlation (r = 0.36, p = 0.005) between COHS scores and app sequence preference.

claim: OCD patients with improved symptomatology after app training had significantly greater preference for the app trained sequence in both experimental conditions compared to patients with unchanged or worsened symptoms.
source: Patients with lowered YBOCS scores after the app training had significantly greater preference for the app trained sequence in both experimental conditions as compared to patients with same or increased YBOCS scores after the app training: experimental condition 1 (pFDR = 0.015, Figure 7c, left) and experimental condition 2 (pFDR = 0.011, Figure 7c, right).
evidence: Supported by post-hoc Dunn's test showing significant differences (pFDR = 0.015 and pFDR = 0.011) between OCD subgroups based on symptom change, with reference to Figure 7c.

claim: The higher the symptom improvement after the month training, the greater the preference for the familiar/learned sequence, particularly when choosing between the trained app sequence and any 3-move sequence.
source: We observed a positive correlation, meaning that the higher the symptom improvement after the month training, the greater the preference for the familiar/learned sequence. This is particularly the case for the experimental condition 2, when subjects are required to choose between the trained app sequence and any 3-move sequence (rs = 0.35, p = 0.04).
evidence: Supported by Spearman correlation analysis showing significant positive correlation (rs = 0.35, p = 0.04) between YBOCS score change and app sequence preference in experimental condition 2.

claim: Both OCD patients and healthy volunteers were highly sensitive to re-evaluation based on monetary feedback, choosing more often the non-app sequence regardless of its novelty.
source: Both groups were highly sensitive to the re-evaluation procedure based on monetary feedback, choosing more often the non-app sequence, irrespective of the novelty of that sequence (Figure 8b, no group effects; p = 0.210 and BF = 0.742, anecdotal evidence supporting no main effect of group).
evidence: Supported by statistical tests showing non-significant group effect (p = 0.210) and Bayesian analysis (BF = 0.742) supporting absence of group differences, with reference to Figure 8b.

claim: When re-evaluation required motor effort, OCD patients significantly favored the trained app sequence over healthy volunteers.
source: However, when re-evaluation required motor effort (condition 4), participants were less inclined to choose the 'any 3' alternative, which is the sequence demanding less motor effort (Kruskal-Wallis main effect of condition: H = 151.1, p < 0.001). Moreover, OCD patients significantly favored the trained app sequence over HV (post hoc group × condition 4 comparison: p = 0.04).
evidence: Supported by Kruskal-Wallis test showing significant main effect of condition (p < 0.001) and post-hoc comparison showing significant group difference in condition 4 (p = 0.04).

claim: The symptom improvement in OCD patients was positively correlated with patients' habitual tendencies reported in the Creature of Habit questionnaire, particularly with the routine subscale.
source: Of note, the symptom improvement was positively correlated with patients' habitual tendencies reported in the Creature of Habit questionnaire, particularly with the routine subscale (Pearson r = 0.45, p = 0.01) (Figure 9a, left).
evidence: Supported by Pearson correlation analysis showing significant positive correlation (r = 0.45, p = 0.01) between YBOCS change and COHS routine subscale, with reference to Figure 9a.

claim: OCD patients who reported less obsessions and compulsions after the month training were the ones with more pronounced habit routines.
source: A three-way ANOVA test showed that patients who reported less obsessions and compulsions after the month training were the ones with more pronounced habit routines (group effect: F = 13.7, p < 0.001, Figure 9a, right).
evidence: Supported by three-way ANOVA showing significant group effect (F = 13.7, p < 0.001) comparing OCD subgroups based on symptom change, with reference to Figure 9a.

claim: OCD patients who considered the app beneficial were the ones with higher compulsivity scores and higher habitual tendencies.
source: A strong positive correlation was also found between the OCD improvement reported subjectively as direct consequence of the app training and the OCI scores and reported habit tendencies (Pearson r = 0.8, p = 0.008; Pearson r = 0.77, p < 0.01, respectively) (Figure 9b): i.e., patients who considered the app somewhat beneficial were the ones with higher compulsivity scores and higher habitual tendencies.
evidence: Supported by Pearson correlation analyses showing strong positive correlations (r = 0.8, p = 0.008 for OCI; r = 0.77, p < 0.01 for COHS) between subjective improvement and clinical measures, with reference to Figure 9b.

claim: In healthy volunteers, participants who had greater tendency for automatic behaviors regarded the app as more relaxing.
source: In HV, participants who also had greater tendency for automatic behaviors, regarded the app as more relaxing (Pearson r = 0.44, p < 0.01).
evidence: Supported by Pearson correlation analysis showing significant positive correlation (r = 0.44, p < 0.01) between COHS automaticity subscale and relaxation rating in HV.

claim: The correlation between self-reported relaxation measure attributed to the app and the COHS automaticity subscale was not observed in OCD patients.
source: However, such correlation between the self-reported relaxation measure attributed to the app and the COHS automaticity subscale was not observed in OCD (p = 0.1).
evidence: Supported by Pearson correlation analysis showing non-significant correlation (p = 0.1) in OCD group.

claim: Patients' symptom improvement did not correlate with how relaxing they considered the app training.
source: Finally, patients' symptom improvement did not correlate with how relaxing they considered the app training (p = 0.1) nor with the number of total practices performed during the month training period (p = 0.2).
evidence: Supported by Pearson correlation analyses showing non-significant correlations (p = 0.1 and p = 0.2) between symptom improvement and relaxation rating or practice number.

claim: OCD patients reported significantly higher intolerance of uncertainty compared to healthy controls.
source: In addition to the Creature of Habit findings, of the remaining self-reported questionnaires assessed (see Materials and methods), OCD patients also reported enhanced intolerance of uncertainty, elevated motivation to avoid aversive outcomes and higher perfectionism, worries and perceived stress, as compared to healthy controls (see Table 1 for statistical results and Figure 10 for overall summary).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparisons (t-tests) showing significant differences between groups on IUS scale, with reference to Table 1 and Figure 10.

claim: OCD patients reported elevated motivation to avoid aversive outcomes compared to healthy controls.
source: In addition to the Creature of Habit findings, of the remaining self-reported questionnaires assessed (see Materials and methods), OCD patients also reported enhanced intolerance of uncertainty, elevated motivation to avoid aversive outcomes and higher perfectionism, worries and perceived stress, as compared to healthy controls (see Table 1 for statistical results and Figure 10 for overall summary).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparisons (t-tests) showing significant differences between groups on BIS scale, with reference to Table 1 and Figure 10.

claim: OCD patients reported higher perfectionism compared to healthy controls.
source: In addition to the Creature of Habit findings, of the remaining self-reported questionnaires assessed (see Materials and methods), OCD patients also reported enhanced intolerance of uncertainty, elevated motivation to avoid aversive outcomes and higher perfectionism, worries and perceived stress, as compared to healthy controls (see Table 1 for statistical results and Figure 10 for overall summary).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparisons (t-tests) showing significant differences between groups on FMPS scale, with reference to Table 1 and Figure 10.

claim: OCD patients reported higher worries compared to healthy controls.
source: In addition to the Creature of Habit findings, of the remaining self-reported questionnaires assessed (see Materials and methods), OCD patients also reported enhanced intolerance of uncertainty, elevated motivation to avoid aversive outcomes and higher perfectionism, worries and perceived stress, as compared to healthy controls (see Table 1 for statistical results and Figure 10 for overall summary).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparisons (t-tests) showing significant differences between groups on PSWQ scale, with reference to Table 1 and Figure 10.

claim: OCD patients reported higher perceived stress compared to healthy controls.
source: In addition to the Creature of Habit findings, of the remaining self-reported questionnaires assessed (see Materials and methods), OCD patients also reported enhanced intolerance of uncertainty, elevated motivation to avoid aversive outcomes and higher perfectionism, worries and perceived stress, as compared to healthy controls (see Table 1 for statistical results and Figure 10 for overall summary).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparisons (t-tests) showing significant differences between groups on PSS scale, with reference to Table 1 and Figure 10.

claim: The goal/habit imbalance theory of compulsion in OCD postulates enhanced habit formation, increased automaticity, and impaired goal/habit arbitration.
source: This study investigates the goal/habit imbalance theory of compulsion in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), which postulates enhanced habit formation, increased automaticity, and impaired goal/habit arbitration.
evidence: This is a statement of the theoretical framework being investigated in the study, representing established theory in the field.

claim: Dysfunctional goal-directed control in OCD has been strongly supported both behaviorally and from a neurobiological perspective.
source: Dysfunctional goal-directed control in OCD has been strongly supported both behaviorally (Gillan et al., 2011; Vaghi et al., 2019) and from a neurobiological perspective (Gillan et al., 2015a).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Gillan et al., 2011; Vaghi et al., 2019; Gillan et al., 2015a) demonstrating dysfunctional goal-directed control in OCD.

claim: Enhanced habit formation in OCD has largely been inferred by the absence of goal-directed control.
source: However, until now, enhanced (and potentially maladaptive) habit formation has largely been inferred by the absence of goal-directed control, although recent studies show increased self-reported habitual tendencies in OCD, as measured by the Self-Report Habit Index Scale (Ferreira et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research (Ferreira et al., 2017) and discussion of how habit formation has been inferred in the field.

claim: Recent findings link stimulus-response strength and goal devaluation exclusively to a dysfunctional goal system.
source: Problems with this 'zero-sum' hypothesis (Robbins and Costa, 2017) (i.e. diminished goal-directed control thus enhanced habitual control) have been reiterated by recent findings linking stimulus-response strength (Zwosta et al., 2018) and goal devaluation (Gillan et al., 2015b) exclusively to a dysfunctional goal system.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Robbins and Costa, 2017; Zwosta et al., 2018; Gillan et al., 2015b) discussing problems with the zero-sum hypothesis.

claim: Extensive training of sequential actions could be a means for rapidly engaging the 'habit system' in a laboratory setting.
source: We recently proposed that extensive training of sequential actions could be a means for rapidly engaging the 'habit system' in a laboratory setting (Robbins et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research (Robbins et al., 2019) proposing this methodological approach.

claim: In action sequences, extensive training helps integrate separate motor actions into a coordinated and unified sequence, or 'chunk'.
source: The idea is that, in action sequences (like those seen in skilled routines), extensive training helps integrate separate motor actions into a coordinated and unified sequence, or 'chunk' (Graybiel, 1998; Sakai et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Graybiel, 1998; Sakai et al., 2003) on action sequence chunking.

claim: For highly trained sequences, actions are represented in parallel according to their serial order before execution.
source: Moreover, there is now robust evidence that for highly trained sequences, actions are represented in parallel according to their serial order before execution (Kornysheva et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research (Kornysheva et al., 2019) on parallel representation of actions in trained sequences.

claim: Automaticity is associated with a shift in control from the anterior/associative (goal-directed) to the posterior/sensorimotor (habitual) striatal regions.
source: At a neural level, automaticity is associated with a shift in control from the anterior/associative (goal-directed) to the posterior/sensorimotor (habitual) striatal regions (Ashby et al., 2010; Graybiel and Grafton, 2015; Kupferschmidt et al., 2017), accompanied by a disengagement of cognitive control hubs in frontal and cingulate cortices (Bassett et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Ashby et al., 2010; Graybiel and Grafton, 2015; Kupferschmidt et al., 2017; Bassett et al., 2015) on neural correlates of automaticity.

claim: Within the skill learning literature, the progressive shift to posterior striatum has been linked to the gradually attained asymptotic performance of the skill.
source: In fact, within the skill learning literature, this progressive shift to posterior striatum has been linked to the gradually attained asymptotic performance of the skill (Bassett et al., 2015; Doyon et al., 2018; Doyon et al., 2015; Lehéricy et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Bassett et al., 2015; Doyon et al., 2018; Doyon et al., 2015; Lehéricy et al., 2005) on skill learning and striatal shifts.

claim: Chunked action sequences provide an opportunity to target the brain's goal-habit transition and study the relationships between automaticity, skills, and habits.
source: Hence, chunked action sequences provide an opportunity to target the brain's goal-habit transition and study the relationships between automaticity, skills, and habits (Dezfouli et al., 2014; Graybiel and Grafton, 2015; Robbins and Costa, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Dezfouli et al., 2014; Graybiel and Grafton, 2015; Robbins and Costa, 2017) on using chunked sequences to study habit formation.

claim: Compulsions in OCD are often performed in a 'just right' manner, akin to skill learning.
source: This approach is relevant for OCD research as it mimics the sequences of motor events and routines observed in typical compulsions, often performed in a ''just right'' manner (Hellriegel et al., 2017), akin to skill learning.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research (Hellriegel et al., 2017) on the 'just right' nature of compulsions in OCD.

claim: The Motor Sequencing App satisfies central criteria that define habits: swift execution, invariant response topography, and action chunking.
source: This task, akin to a piano-based app, allows subjects to learn and practice two sequences of finger movements. It was tailored to emphasize the positive aspects of habits, as advocated by Watson et al., 2022, and it satisfies central criteria that define habits proposed by Balleine and Dezfouli, 2019: swift execution, invariant response topography, and action chunking.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Watson et al., 2022; Balleine and Dezfouli, 2019) defining criteria for habits.

claim: The autonomous nature of habits and the fluid proficiency of skills engage the same sensorimotor cortical-striatal 'loops' (the so-called 'habit circuitry').
source: Although there is no consensus on how exactly skills and habits interact (Robbins and Costa, 2017), it is generally agreed that both lead to automaticity with sufficient practice (Graybiel and Grafton, 2015) and that the autonomous nature of habits and the fluid proficiency of skills engage the same sensorimotor cortical-striatal 'loops' (the so-called 'habit circuitry') (Ashby et al., 2010; Graybiel and Grafton, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Robbins and Costa, 2017; Graybiel and Grafton, 2015; Ashby et al., 2010) on the relationship between habits, skills, and neural circuitry.

claim: Outcome devaluation insensitivity as a test of habit in humans is controversial and may be a more sensitive indicator of failures of goal-directed control rather than of habitual control per se.
source: This is important because outcome devaluation insensitivity as a test of habit in humans is controversial (Watson et al., 2022) and may indeed be a more sensitive indicator of failures of goal-directed control rather than of habitual control per se (Balleine and Dezfouli, 2019; Robbins et al., 2019; Robbins and Costa, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Watson et al., 2022; Balleine and Dezfouli, 2019; Robbins et al., 2019; Robbins and Costa, 2017) discussing controversies around devaluation tests.

claim: Training frequency, context stability, and reward contingencies are important features for enhancing habit strength.
source: While designing our app, we additionally considered previous research emphasizing training frequency, context stability, and reward contingencies as important features for enhancing habit strength (Wood and Rünger, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research (Wood and Rünger, 2016) on factors enhancing habit strength.

claim: Practice alone is insufficient for habit development as it also requires off-line consolidation over longer periods of time and sleep.
source: To ensure effective consolidation required for habit/skill retention to occur, we implemented a 1-month training period. This aligns with studies showing that practice alone is insufficient for habit development as it also requires off-line consolidation over longer periods of time and sleep (Nusbaum et al., 2018; Walker et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Nusbaum et al., 2018; Walker et al., 2003) on the role of consolidation and sleep in habit development.

claim: Reinforcer predictability influences habit acquisition speed.
source: Finally, given the influence of reinforcer predictability on habit acquisition speed (Bouton, 2021), we employed two different reinforcement schedules (reward scores: continuous versus variable [probabilistic]) to assess their impact on habit formation among healthy volunteers (HV) and patients with OCD.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research (Bouton, 2021) on the influence of reinforcer predictability on habit acquisition.

claim: Implicit learning issues have been reported in OCD.
source: Anticipating implicit learning issues in OCD (Deckersbach et al., 2002; Kathmann et al., 2005; Rauch et al., 1997) and fine-motor difficulties (Bloch et al., 2011), we expected poorer procedural learning in patients compared to HV.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Deckersbach et al., 2002; Kathmann et al., 2005; Rauch et al., 1997) reporting implicit learning issues in OCD.

claim: Fine-motor difficulties have been reported in OCD.
source: Anticipating implicit learning issues in OCD (Deckersbach et al., 2002; Kathmann et al., 2005; Rauch et al., 1997) and fine-motor difficulties (Bloch et al., 2011), we expected poorer procedural learning in patients compared to HV.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research (Bloch et al., 2011) reporting fine-motor difficulties in OCD.

claim: OCD patients have heightened sensitivity to negative feedback.
source: Additionally, we predicted that OCD patients would generally display stronger habits and assign greater intrinsic value to the familiar app sequences, evidenced by a marked preference for executing them even when presented with a simpler alternative sequences. Finally, we expected patients to show a greater tendency to perform the familiar/trained sequences, even though its extrinsic relative value was reduced and new, more valuable, options became available.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Apergis-Schoute et al., 2024; Becker et al., 2014; Kanen et al., 2019) on heightened sensitivity to negative feedback in OCD, mentioned earlier in the manuscript.

claim: The tendency to attribute higher intrinsic value to familiar actions may be a potential mechanism leading to compulsions and an important addition to the goal/habit imbalance hypothesis in OCD.
source: The tendency to attribute higher intrinsic value to familiar actions may be a potential mechanism leading to compulsions and an important addition to the goal/habit imbalance hypothesis in OCD.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation and conclusion drawn from the study's findings, representing the authors' inference about mechanisms underlying compulsions.

claim: Smartphone app training has potential as a habit reversal therapeutic tool.
source: We also highlight the potential of smartphone app training as a habit reversal therapeutic tool.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the exploratory findings of symptom improvement in some OCD patients, suggesting potential therapeutic applications.

claim: The repeated performance of motor sequences could develop implicit rewarding properties, hence gaining value, potentially leading to compulsive-like behaviors.
source: The first research question investigated whether repeated performance of motor sequences could develop implicit rewarding properties, hence gaining value, potentially leading to compulsive-like behaviors (experiment 2: explicit preference task, conducted without feedback). The hypothesis postulates that the repeated performance, initially driven by the goal of proficiency, may eventually become motivated by its own implicit reward, tied to proprioceptive and kinesthetic feedback (e.g. offering anxiety relief alongside skillful execution).
evidence: This is a hypothesis being tested in the study, representing a speculative mechanism for how repeated actions might gain intrinsic value.

claim: Context change promotes re-engagement of the goal system.
source: These tasks were conducted in a new context, which has been shown to promote re-engagement of the goal system (Bouton, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research (Bouton, 2021) on the effect of context change on goal system engagement.

claim: Habit 'replacement' hypothesis is in line with successful interventions in Tourette syndrome, tic disorders, and trichotillomania.
source: One hypothesis for the therapeutic potential of this motor sequencing training is that the trained action sequences may disrupt OCD compulsions, either via 'distraction' or habit 'replacement', by engaging the same neural 'habit circuitry'. This habit 'replacement' hypothesis is in line with successful interventions in Tourette syndrome (Hwang et al., 2012), tic disorders (Bate et al., 2011), and trichotillomania (Morris et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Hwang et al., 2012; Bate et al., 2011; Morris et al., 2013) on successful habit replacement interventions in related disorders.

claim: The study successfully achieved automaticity, fulfilling three of the four criteria for the definition of habits according to Balleine and Dezfouli, 2019 (rapid execution, invariant topography, and chunked action sequences).
source: We succeeded in achieving automaticity – which at a neural level is known to reliably engage the brain's habitual circuitry (Ashby et al., 2010; Bassett et al., 2015; Graybiel and Grafton, 2015; Lehéricy et al., 2005) – and fulfilled three of the four criteria for the definition of habits according to Balleine and Dezfouli, 2019 (rapid execution, invariant topography, and chunked action sequences).
evidence: Based on inference from the data showing achievement of automaticity criteria, with citations to supporting literature (Ashby et al., 2010; Bassett et al., 2015; Graybiel and Grafton, 2015; Lehéricy et al., 2005; Balleine and Dezfouli, 2019).

claim: The study was unable to test the fourth criterion of resistance to devaluation for defining habits.
source: However, we were not able to test the fourth criterion of resistance to devaluation. Therefore, we are unable to firmly conclude that the action sequences are habits rather than, for example, goal-directed skills.
evidence: This is an explicit acknowledgment of a limitation in the study design.

claim: Overtraining of a three-element sequence with less training has been shown to achieve behavioral autonomy from the goal.
source: According to a very recent study, also employing an app to study habitual behavior, the criterion of devaluation resistance was shown to apply to a three-element sequence with less training (Gera et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research (Gera et al., 2022) showing devaluation resistance in shorter sequences with less training.

claim: The app-trained sequences encompass both habitual and goal-directed qualities, aligning with contemporary perspectives on skilled/habitual sequences.
source: While this interpretation holds merit, the logical conclusion is that the app-trained sequences encompass both habitual and goal-directed qualities. This aligns with contemporary perspectives on skilled/habitual sequences (Du and Haith, 2023).
evidence: Based on inference from the study findings and supported by citation to contemporary perspectives (Du and Haith, 2023).

claim: Behavior in general is 'goal-directed' but may vary in the balance of control by external and internal goals.
source: One implication of this analysis may be to consider that behavior in general is 'goal-directed' but may vary in the balance of control by external and internal goals.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation and speculation about the nature of goal-directed behavior based on the study findings.

claim: The dual associative process framework of behavioral control might be better understood in terms of the relative importance of extrinsic versus intrinsic outcomes.
source: In light of these insights, the dual associative process framework of behavioral control might be better understood in terms of the relative importance of extrinsic versus intrinsic outcomes.
evidence: This is a theoretical reinterpretation of the dual process framework based on the study findings, representing speculation about how to conceptualize behavioral control.

claim: Habits, which depend initially on cached or historically acquired rewarding action values, may not necessarily lose current value, but instead acquire alternative sources of value.
source: Another possible formulation is that habits, which depend initially on cached or historically acquired rewarding action values, may not necessarily lose current value, but instead acquire alternative sources of value (Hommel and Wiers, 2017; Kruglanski and Szumowska, 2020; O'Doherty, 2014).
evidence: This is a theoretical speculation about the nature of habit value, supported by citations to previous theoretical work (Hommel and Wiers, 2017; Kruglanski and Szumowska, 2020; O'Doherty, 2014).

claim: The finding of no procedural learning deficits in OCD patients is inconsistent with other implicit learning deficits previously reported in OCD using the serial reaction time paradigm.
source: However, despite this initial slowness, no procedural learning deficits were found in our patient sample. This finding is inconsistent with other implicit learning deficits previously reported in OCD using the serial reaction time (SRT) paradigm (Deckersbach et al., 2002; Joel et al., 2005; Kathmann et al., 2005; Rauch et al., 2001; Rauch et al., 1997).
evidence: Based on comparison of current findings with previous research cited (Deckersbach et al., 2002; Joel et al., 2005; Kathmann et al., 2005; Rauch et al., 2001; Rauch et al., 1997).

claim: The current result aligns with recent studies demonstrating successful learning in OCD patients and individuals with subclinical OCD symptoms when instructions are given explicitly.
source: Nevertheless, this result aligns with recent studies demonstrating successful learning both in patients with OCD (Soref et al., 2018) and in healthy individuals with subclinical OCD symptoms (Barzilay et al., 2022) when instructions are given explicitly, and participants intentionally search for the underlying sequence structure.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Soref et al., 2018; Barzilay et al., 2022) showing successful learning in OCD with explicit instructions.

claim: The current task does not tap into memory processes as strongly as SRT tasks because the sequence is explicitly demonstrated to participants before training.
source: In fact, our task does not tap into memory processes as strongly as SRT tasks because we explicitly demonstrate the sequence to participants before they begin their 30-day training, which likely decreases demands on procedural learning.
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of the task and its cognitive demands compared to other paradigms.

claim: A heightened sensitivity to negative feedback within the motor domain has been documented in the general population, influencing initial motor improvements.
source: A heightened sensitivity to negative feedback within the motor domain has been documented in the general population, influencing initial motor improvements, while an increase in reward primarily boosts motor retention (Abe et al., 2011; Galea et al., 2015; Pekny et al., 2015; van Mastrigt et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Abe et al., 2011; Galea et al., 2015; Pekny et al., 2015; van Mastrigt et al., 2020) on sensitivity to negative feedback in motor learning.

claim: The current findings do not support differences in OCD and healthy individuals with regard to sensitivity to negative score changes, unlike previous work highlighting increased response switching after negative feedback in OCD.
source: Our results, however, do not support differences in OCD and healthy individuals with regard to sensitivity to negative score changes, unlike previous work highlighting increased response switching after negative feedback, hyperactive monitoring systems, and amplified prediction errors in OCD (Hauser et al., 2017; Marzuki et al., 2021).
evidence: Based on comparison of current findings with previous research cited (Hauser et al., 2017; Marzuki et al., 2021), representing an inference about differences between studies.

claim: Previous studies have reported that subjective habitual tendencies are associated with compulsive traits.
source: Previous studies have reported that subjective habitual tendencies are associated with compulsive traits (Ersche et al., 2019; Wuensch et al., 2022) and act, in addition to cognitive inflexibility, as a predictor of subclinical OCD symptomatology in healthy populations (Ramakrishnan et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Ersche et al., 2019; Wuensch et al., 2022; Ramakrishnan et al., 2022) on the relationship between habitual tendencies and compulsive traits.

claim: The habit 'replacement' hypothesis suggests that trained action sequences may disrupt OCD compulsions by engaging the same neural 'habit circuitry'.
source: One hypothesis for the therapeutic potential of this motor sequencing training is that the trained action sequences may disrupt OCD compulsions, either via 'distraction' or habit 'replacement', by engaging the same neural 'habit circuitry'.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain potential therapeutic effects.

claim: The study was unable to employ the 'gold standard' criterion of resistance to devaluation because it would have invalidated subsequent tests.
source: As mentioned above, we were unable to employ the often-mooted 'gold standard' criterion of resistance to devaluation because it would have invalidated the subsequent tests.
evidence: This is an explicit acknowledgment of a methodological limitation and the reasoning behind it.

claim: The utility of the devaluation criterion has been questioned especially when applied to human studies of habit learning.
source: Nevertheless, the utility of the devaluation criterion has been questioned especially when applied to human studies of habit learning. This is because achieving devaluation can be difficult given that human behavior has multiple goals, some of which may be implicit, and thus difficult to control experimentally, as well as being subject to great individual variation.
evidence: This represents established knowledge and ongoing debate in the field about methodological issues with devaluation tests.

claim: Recent analyses of habitual behavior have not employed devaluation or revaluation as a criterion.
source: In fact recent analyses of habitual behavior have not employed devaluation or revaluation as a criterion (Du and Haith, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent research (Du and Haith, 2023) on alternative approaches to studying habitual behavior.

claim: The 'monetary discounting' condition involved a simple deterministic choice between two alternatives with non-overlapping reward ranges.
source: However, it may have arisen because of the nature of the contingencies inherent in these choice tests. Specifically, the 'monetary discounting' condition involved a simple deterministic choice between the two alternatives, which should readily be resolved in favor of the option associated with the greater, non-overlapping, range of rewards provided (e.g. 1–7 versus 8–15 gems).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and an inference about why it may have been easier to resolve.

claim: In the 'effort discounting' condition, the reward ranges for the two options were equivalent, which raised uncertainty concerning which of the chosen sequences was optimal.
source: In contrast, in the 'effort discounting' condition, the reward ranges for the two options were equivalent (e.g. 1–7 gems), which raised uncertainty concerning which of the chosen sequences was optimal.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and an inference about how it created uncertainty.

claim: The probabilistic constraint in the effort discounting condition may account for the greater sensitivity of the task in highlighting preference in OCD, given the greater susceptibility of such patients to uncertainty.
source: The probabilistic constraint over this choice may therefore account for the greater sensitivity of the task in highlighting preference in OCD, given the greater susceptibility of such patients to uncertainty (Pushkarskaya et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference about why the task was more sensitive in OCD, supported by citation to previous research (Pushkarskaya et al., 2015) on uncertainty in OCD.

claim: The study recruited 33 OCD patients and 34 healthy individuals, matched for age, gender, IQ, and years of education.
source: We recruited 33 OCD patients and 34 healthy individuals, matched for age, gender, IQ, and years of education.
evidence: This is a description of the study sample and matching procedure.

claim: Two participants (one HV and one OCD) were excluded because they did not perform the minimum required training.
source: Two participants (one HV and one OCD) were excluded because they did not perform the minimum required training (i.e. two daily practices for a period of 30 days).
evidence: This is a description of participant exclusions and the criteria used.

claim: A total of 32 OCD patients (19 females) and 33 healthy participants (19 females) were included in the analysis.
source: Therefore, a total of 32 OCD patients (19 females) and 33 healthy participants (19 females) were included in the analysis.
evidence: This is a description of the final sample size and composition.

claim: Most participants were right-handed (left-handed: four OCD and six HV).
source: Most participants were right-handed (left-handed: four OCD and six HV).
evidence: This is a description of participant handedness distribution.
